title: Rich Habits Poor Habits (Sự Khác Biệt Giữa Người Giàu Và Người Nghèo)
author: Tom Corley & Michael Yardney
summary:
Rich Habits Poor Habits combines two distinct bodies of work: Tom Corley's original research tracking the daily habits of 233 self-made rich individuals against 128 people living in poverty, and Michael Yardney's parallel expertise in wealth psychology and property investing, adapted here for an international (and in this Vietnamese edition, Vietnamese-market) audience. The book's premise is that wealth is far less about intelligence, luck, or inherited advantage than it is about accumulated daily habits — specific, identifiable, repeatable behaviors that compound over years into either financial security or financial struggle, largely below the level of conscious daily decision-making.

The book opens by making the case for why an ordinary reader should believe wealth is achievable through habit change rather than circumstance, then spends its middle section building the psychological foundation: how mindset shapes financial behavior, why most people never develop the specific thinking patterns of the wealthy, and the neuroscience-adjacent explanations (attention, delayed gratification, belief systems) the authors offer for why some habits are so hard to change without deliberate intervention.

The bulk of the book is then organized around Corley's specific "Rich Habits" — a defined list of concrete daily practices drawn from his original research (things like goal-setting practices, reading habits, relationship and networking behaviors, financial discipline around saving and spending, and health routines) presented as short, focused chapters, each explaining one habit, why the data suggests it correlates with wealth accumulation, and how to build it. Yardney's property investment expertise is layered in throughout as the applied wealth-building context for readers who have adopted the underlying habits and mindset and are ready to act on them.

The book's overall arc moves from persuasion (wealth is achievable) to psychology (why habits are hard and how to change them) to a concrete, checklist-like inventory of specific habits to adopt, closing with practical guidance oriented toward property investment as Yardney's preferred wealth-building vehicle for readers who have internalized the earlier material.

sections.title: Why We Want You to Become Rich
sections.summary:
This opening section makes the book's foundational case: that wealth is achievable for ordinary readers, not just the already-advantaged, and introduces both authors' backgrounds and credibility — Corley's original habit research and Yardney's standing as an Australian wealth psychology and property investment authority.

The authors position the rest of the book as a practical, evidence-informed alternative to vague motivational wealth advice, promising specific, research-backed habits rather than generic encouragement, while being explicit that becoming rich requires sustained behavior change, not a single insight or decision.

The section closes by previewing the book's three-part structure — mindset foundations, the specific Rich Habits program, and applied wealth-building guidance — that the rest of the book works through in sequence.
keyLessons: Treat wealth-building as a matter of sustained behavior change, not a single decision or insight.
Evaluate wealth advice by whether it offers something specific and research-grounded, not just generic motivation.
Expect the book's guidance to build cumulatively across mindset, specific habits, and applied investing.

sections.title: Developing a Rich Mindset
sections.summary:
This section builds the psychological foundation for the specific habits to come, covering how mindset shapes financial behavior — including the idea that people largely control their own financial destiny through their thinking patterns, common limiting beliefs that keep people financially stuck, and why most people never develop the mental habits the authors associate with wealth.

The authors cover concepts like selective attention (the idea that your brain filters for what you're primed to notice, which shapes what financial opportunities you even perceive) and work through "ways the rich think differently" as a contrast set against common limiting beliefs about money and self-worth.

The section closes by connecting mindset to the delayed-gratification research referenced throughout the book, arguing that the capacity to delay gratification is itself a trainable habit rather than a fixed trait, setting up the book's shift from mindset to concrete habit-building.
keyLessons: Recognize that selective attention shapes which financial opportunities you even notice — and that this can be deliberately trained.
Identify and challenge specific limiting beliefs about money that may be operating below conscious awareness.
Treat delayed gratification as a trainable habit, not a fixed personality trait you either have or don't.

sections.title: The Rich Habits Program
sections.summary:
This central section introduces and works through Corley's specific Rich Habits — the concrete, research-derived daily practices distinguishing the self-made rich individuals in his study from the people living in poverty he also studied — covering areas including goal-setting, reading and continuous learning, relationship and networking habits, financial discipline (saving, budgeting, avoiding lifestyle inflation), and health routines that support sustained mental and physical energy.

Each habit is presented as a short, focused unit explaining the specific behavior, the reasoning or research basis behind its correlation with wealth, and practical guidance for building it into a daily routine, allowing readers to adopt them incrementally rather than all at once.

The section closes by acknowledging that habit change is genuinely difficult and gradual, and that readers should expect to build these habits progressively over time rather than attempting to adopt the full list simultaneously, transitioning into the book's closing section on applying these habits toward actual wealth-building.
keyLessons: Adopt Rich Habits incrementally rather than attempting to overhaul your entire routine at once.
Prioritize the specific habit categories the research emphasizes: goal-setting, reading, relationships, financial discipline, and health.
Expect habit change to be gradual and treat early setbacks as normal, not evidence the approach isn't working.

sections.title: Applying the Habits: Wealth-Building in Practice
sections.summary:
This closing section shifts from habit-building to applied wealth creation, drawing primarily on Yardney's property investment expertise as the concrete vehicle through which readers who have adopted the earlier mindset and habits can actually build measurable wealth.

The authors connect the psychological and habit-based groundwork of earlier sections directly to practical financial decision-making, arguing that habits and mindset without an actual investment vehicle produce discipline without results, while an investment vehicle without the underlying habits and mindset tends to be squandered or poorly executed.

The book closes by reiterating its central thesis: that the daily, unglamorous, and highly specific habits documented throughout the book — not talent, luck, or a single big break — are what actually separate people who build lasting wealth from people who don't, regardless of starting point.
keyLessons: Pair the mindset and habit work from earlier sections with an actual investment vehicle to convert discipline into results.
Recognize that an investment strategy without supporting habits and mindset is likely to be poorly executed or squandered.
Treat consistent daily habits, not a single decision or windfall, as the real long-term driver of wealth accumulation.
Treat wealth-building as the product of sustained daily habits compounding over years, not a single decision or windfall.
Train your attention deliberately, since what you're primed to notice shapes which financial opportunities you perceive.
Identify and actively challenge limiting beliefs about money that operate below conscious awareness.
Build the capacity for delayed gratification as a trainable habit rather than accepting it as a fixed trait.
Adopt specific Rich Habits incrementally across goal-setting, reading, relationships, financial discipline, and health.
Expect habit change to be gradual, and treat early setbacks as normal rather than as proof the approach has failed.
Pair habit and mindset work with an actual investment vehicle to convert discipline into measurable financial results.
Prioritize consistency over intensity — small, repeated daily behaviors outperform occasional large efforts.

whoThisIsFor: Readers who want a specific, checklist-style set of daily habits to adopt, rather than abstract motivational advice about becoming wealthy.
whenToReadThis: Read it when you're ready to commit to changing daily routines over months, not when looking for a quick financial fix.

authorBio.name: Tom Corley & Michael Yardney
authorBio.bio:
Tom Corley is an American author and researcher known for his multi-year study of the daily habits of self-made rich individuals compared with people living in poverty, published originally in his book Rich Habits, which became the foundation for the habit-research content in this collaborative title.

Michael Yardney is an Australian property investment expert and commentator widely known in Australia for his work on the psychology of wealth creation and success, including mentoring and educating property investors, and for his own separate body of published work on real estate investing.

The two authors combined Corley's original habit research with Yardney's wealth psychology and property investment expertise to produce Rich Habits Poor Habits as an internationally adapted, expanded edition aimed at a broader audience than either author's original solo work.

How to Grow a Multi-Million Dollar Property Portfolio (Michael Yardney)

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Rich Habits Program
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Tom Corley's research-derived set of specific daily habits — spanning goal-setting, reading, relationship-building, financial discipline, and health routines — identified through his study comparing 233 self-made rich individuals against 128 people living in poverty, and presented as learnable, adoptable behaviors rather than fixed personality traits.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Selective Attention / Reticular Activating System
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The book's framing of the brain's attention-filtering mechanism as something that can be deliberately trained to notice financial opportunities and information consistent with a wealth-building mindset, rather than passively filtering the world according to old, limiting beliefs.

actionSteps: Choose one specific Rich Habit from the book (for example, a daily reading habit or a written goal-setting practice) and commit to it for 30 days before adding another.
Write down three limiting beliefs about money you notice in your own thinking, and write a specific counter-statement for each.
Practice one deliberate delayed-gratification exercise this week — choosing a smaller immediate reward over a larger later one — and note how it felt.
Identify one concrete investment vehicle (property, index funds, a small business) you could realistically pair with your new habits once they're established.
reflectionQuestions: Which of your current daily habits, if continued unchanged for ten years, would move you toward or away from financial security?
What limiting belief about money did you absorb early in life, and where do you still see it shaping your decisions today?

points: Corley's underlying research sample (233 rich individuals and 128 people in poverty) is relatively small and self-selected, and the book presents correlational habit data as if it demonstrates causation — readers should treat "the rich do X" as an observed pattern, not proof that adopting X alone will produce wealth.

Several reader reviews note the book reads as two loosely merged works (Corley's habit research and Yardney's property investing material) rather than a single unified argument, with some repetition across chapters as a result.

The book's habit-based framework understates the role of structural and starting-point factors (access to capital, inherited advantage, geography, discrimination) in wealth outcomes, treating habit adoption as sufficient on its own regardless of starting conditions.

Yardney's applied wealth-building guidance leans heavily toward property investment specifically, which may not suit every reader's market, risk tolerance, or capital position, despite being presented as the book's primary applied wealth vehicle.
criticalTake.contextNote: As an internationally licensed and translated title, this Vietnamese edition adapts source material originally researched primarily in the US (Corley) and Australia (Yardney); some specific financial and property-market detail may reflect those markets rather than Vietnamese conditions.

sourceNotes:
Synthesis is based on general knowledge of habit-based wealth psychology research plus web-verified publisher, retailer, and reader-review descriptions confirming the book's three-part structure (mindset foundations, the specific Rich Habits program organized as short numbered-habit chapters, and applied property-investment guidance) and both authors' backgrounds. Individual "Rich Habit Number" micro-chapters (roughly 30 in the original table of contents) have been grouped into one representative section rather than given 30 separate near-identical entries, since each is only a page or two in the source book — flagged here for transparency. Quote availability for direct verbatim lines from this specific title is thin, so only one representative line is included.
